I'm a collections attorney in Miami, and my week is usually very organized. On Mondays, I read the new cases and I call the clients. Our firm usually represents creditors: banks, hospitals and small businesses. From Tuesday to Thursday, I write letters to debtors and I prepare documents for the court. On Fridays, I check every deadline for the next week, because a missed deadline can lose a case. But this month is different. I'm working on a case with a team in Brazil, so I'm having meetings at seven in the morning, and I'm learning a lot about Brazilian law.

For six years, I only handled local cases, here in England. Then I moved to a firm with clients in twelve countries. The law was not the hardest part. The hardest part was the meetings. People spoke fast, with different accents, and I was afraid to ask questions. I thought everybody understood everything. Of course, they didn't. Today I manage a team, and I always tell new lawyers the same thing. Ask questions, even simple ones. Nobody knows everything in an international case, and everybody is learning, all the time.

In my job, I see the same story every week. A company borrows money, everything is fine for a year, and then it stops paying. First, we call the client and we try to find a solution, like a new payment plan. Many companies accept, and the problem ends there. But some don't answer. Every month, the outstanding debt grows, because of interest and fees. After ninety days without a payment, we send the case to a law firm. From that moment, the lawyers handle everything. They know the courts, the deadlines and the rules. We just wait for the good news.
